newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW - Shangri-La bullish about 1997.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Shangri-La bullish about 1997.

text.p: Asian hotel owner Shangri-La Asia Ltd said on Thursday it expected to see revenue growth from most of its hotels in the region but a question mark hung over the key China market.
"We look forward to a very good year in 1997," managing director Paul Bush said in an interview.

"I think that there will certainly be growth in Hong Kong over '96. And in other areas of the region, we will expect to have growth," he said. "China, we hope we'll recover...but it's too early to tell."
The group owns two operating hotels in Hong Kong, 10 in China, three in the Philippines, one in Indonesia and two in Fiji. The British colony of Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule on July 1.
In the first quarter of 1996, China contributed 42 percent of the group's operating profit and Hong Kong 35 percent, said financial controller Frankie Heng.
Bush said the China market, which became progressively softer last year, especially in Beijing and Shanghai, could stay soft this year.
"We are looking for growth anywhere, but China will remain some degree soft," the managing director said.
Factors that affected the sector last year could continue to be problems this year, Heng said.

They were: reduced average length of stay due to higher flight frequency, slower investment in China under a prolonged austerity plan and a fall in the number of trade and political delegations visiting China, he said.
The group plans to open 10 more China hotels in coming years.
Its seven China hotels opened before 1996 achieved an average occupancy of 70 percent in the first 11 months of last year, unchanged from the same period in 1995, Heng said.
Bush said he expected the group to fare well in other parts of Asia this year, after being consistently strong last year.
The 1997 outlook for Hong Kong was very bright, he said, with the handover and other functions including the World Bank meeting in September expected to draw extra visitors.
"We feel very strongly about the future, the success and prosperity of Hong Kong after the handover," he said.
"And we'll continue to participate in expansion in Hong Kong..."

The firm had expressed an interest in developing two three- to four-star hotels around the Tai Kok Tsui station on the future airport rail-link, and would submit a bid if shortlisted by the project owner, Bush said.
The company's two Hong Kong hotels, both five-star, saw an average occupancy rate of 82 percent in the first 11 months of last year, versus 78 in the year-earlier period, Heng said.

In the first 11 months of last year, the Philippine hotels had an average occupancy of 82 percent, versus 77 percent in the year-ago period. The Jakarta hotel saw occupancy of 75 percent from January to November, 1996, versus 59 percent a year ago.
Its Fiji hotels would continue to benefit from their 1995 renovation, Bush said. They had average occupancy of 71 percent in the first 11 months of 1996, versus 59 percent previously.

He said the company had a comfortable financial standing, with total net debt to equity ratio below 25 percent at the end of December, cash funds of HK$1 billion (US$129.2 million), convertible bonds of HK$1.8 billion and bank debts of about US$2 billion.
